extracted.intended_audience: fiction and nonfiction writers seeking guidance on using peer critique and professional editing for manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when to use peer critique versus paid professional editing, how to choose and manage different kinds of readers/editors, and how to apply feedback effectively during the revision process.

rubrics_metrics.name: When peer feedback is useful
rubrics_metrics.description: This type of feedback can be useful when: You’re in the early stage of a writing project (or writing career) and trying to find your way; You want to test out ideas before investing too much time and energy; You find that you learn by critiquing others; You work best when you have ongoing support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer feedback is typically free and reciprocal, usually given in chunks rather than on the whole manuscript. Its utility depends on the skill, candor, and sensitivity of the people involved. Don’t assume novice status equals worthless feedback—sensitive readers can spot gaps even if they aren’t accomplished writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and pitfalls of peer critique groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer responses can be “too kind” (to avoid discouraging) or inappropriately harsh, or reflect how the reader would have written the scene rather than objective issues; among inexperienced groups this can be 'the blind leading the blind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of personal opinion vs substantive critique. Expect variability and possible bias. If several people point out the same problem, treat it seriously; but don’t adopt every suggestion. Learn to be discriminating rather than defensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indications it’s time for professional (paid) feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider paid professional feedback if: peers haven’t helped with concerns; peer responses are 'consistently inconsistent' and causing confusion or paralysis; external factors (deadlines) require faster or more thorough evaluation; or you feel a paid professional’s response is more legitimate and necessary to sufficiently scrutinize and perfect the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no ironclad rule—use these indications as signals. Paid feedback can provide clarity and thoroughness that peers may not, especially when impartial, expert judgment is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and scope of professional editing services
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors’ services can include a detailed narrative report, line edits on every page, a follow-up phone conversation, or a general assessment of strengths and weaknesses; fees may be hourly or task-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this is a business relationship, get mutual clarity on what you're buying. Beware of vague feedback, late delivery, or editors who list problems but only offer fixes at extra cost. Ask for sample pages or a trial period to assess scope and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a professional editor (fit and qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you hire a professional editor, make sure she is knowledgeable about your genre and can provide recent, trustworthy references. Ideally ask for a trial period or sample pages to assess fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview editors about their specific experience, request references, and check whether they allow follow-up conversation. Assess your own willingness to listen—good editors often deliver 'a big wallop of tough love.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify expectations and contract with an editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Have mutual clarity about what you’re purchasing — scope of edits, timeline, deliverables, and fees — to avoid disappointment or feeling 'ripped off.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request clear deliverables (e.g., narrative report vs line edits), deadlines, and whether additional tasks will cost more. Consider a trial sample so both parties confirm expectations before committing to a full job.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to seek a second professional opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Get a second editor’s opinion when you want a fresh look from someone not influenced by prior versions, or when you believe the first editor left gaps the second could fill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Is there a specific aspect the first editor couldn’t evaluate? Are there sound reasons the first editor was a poor choice for you? Is the first editor unavailable or unable to give an impartial reading? Multiple perspectives can balance one another, but avoid endlessly seeking reassurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid beta readers vs. paid editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid beta readers typically cost less and will tell you what’s not working but not necessarily how to fix it; they are skilled readers rather than writing instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beta readers are often most useful after a major revision to confirm whether changes have succeeded and to point out remaining issues. Services may vary in checklist items and depth; you can hire individuals or use middleman services to match you with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of specialized readers: sensitivity readers, copy editors, proofreaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers check representation and authenticity of groups (not craft elements); copy editors attend to grammar and surface-level concerns including overused words and continuity 'gaps and goofs'; proofreaders correct typos, misspellings, and style inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the right specialist for the right task: sensitivity readers for cultural authenticity, copy editors for style/continuity, proofreaders for final error clean-up. Know that each role has a distinct remit and won’t substitute for developmental editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace yourself when managing feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t ask for too much at once; focus on one major aspect at a time where possible and digest feedback before requesting more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tackling too many changes simultaneously can be overwhelming. Sequence revisions (e.g., structure first, then line-level work) and allow time to absorb criticism productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try suggested changes experimentally ('Try it on')
rubrics_metrics.description: Before rejecting a suggestion outright, play with changing your story the way the reviewer suggested to see how it feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may discover that a change works or that you prefer a different solution; the act of trying can reveal insights and avoids reflexive dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize feedback systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize feedback and put it into categories (e.g., pacing, character relationships), and consider dating feedback to track how you've addressed elements across drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping organized notes helps you see patterns across reviewers and over time. Categorization aids prioritization and tracking of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize problem identification over suggested solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay more attention to identification of problems than to reviewers’ particular proposed solutions; different reviewers may offer different fixes but consistent problem identification signals something you need to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reviewers’ solutions as input rather than prescriptions. Often you’ll create your own, better solution once you understand the underlying issue (e.g., stakes, motivation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the source of feedback (bias awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of potential biases in readers’ perceptions (preferences, genre tastes) and your own biases (e.g., 'I paid so much so she must be right').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feedback conflicts, step back and analyze why perspectives differ. Evaluate whether a reader’s preferences or relationship to you might color their comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow time and distance before applying all feedback ('Come back later')
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes you’ll see things differently after stepping away from the manuscript for a while.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return with fresh eyes to evaluate feedback and edits; initial emotional reactions can subside and new clarity may emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep all feedback (do not discard immediately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even comments you’re certain are wrong should be set aside rather than thrown away; revisit them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback that seems irrelevant now might reveal patterns across projects or be useful in future drafts or future books. Treat feedback as a learning resource, even if the lesson isn’t immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be discriminating, not defensive, about suggested changes
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t have to adopt every suggestion, but if several people point to the same problem, it probably is one to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance openness with critical judgment. Distinguish between defensiveness and thoughtful selection of which suggestions to implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t hire an editor solely to mimic a target publisher’s taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying to find an editor who will shape your manuscript specifically to what you imagine a dream publisher wants is not the most helpful approach; publishers accept books for varied reasons and often prefer something fresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on making the book as good as possible and finding an editor who is smart, experienced, and whom you trust to bring out your manuscript’s strengths rather than chasing assumed publisher preferences.
